newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia plants say Ukraine alumina talks break down.
newsitem.headline: Russia plants say Ukraine alumina talks break down.

text.p: Russia's two biggest aluminium smelters, Bratsk and Krasnoyarsk, have broken off talks with Ukraine's Mykolayiv alumina plant because of a disagreement over prices, senior officials at the smelters said on Thursday.
Discussions may resume in March, but the smelters said they would look for raw material supplies outside the Commonwealth of Independent States to cover their 1997 needs.

"Unfortunately we cannot agree on the price, and their (Mykolayiv's) price is higher than world prices," Yuri Shlaifshtein, a board member at the world's largest aluminium smelter, Bratsk, told Reuters.
"We say now we will buy alumina outside the CIS. There it is much cheaper," said Gennady Druzhinin, board chairman at Krasnoyarsk, the world's second biggest plant.

Shlaifshtein said the gap between buyer and seller was between $35 and $40 per tonne, but would not elaborate on outright prices. He said Mykolayiv's prices were inflated by high production costs and an overall lack of competitiveness.
But he also said Bratsk may renew talks in March.
"We do not plan to renew negoatiations before the beginning of March," he said.
Druzhinin said that the break-down in discussions between the two sides was costing his plant money.
"We are losing money, because abroad the price of alumina is rising," he added.
Prices have firmed lately to around $185/190 a tonne, fob Australia, from $140/145 in the third quarter last year, Macquarie Equities said in a recent report.
Both Bratsk and Krasnonyarsk said that they have covered most of their alumina requirements for 1997, but some purchases still needed to be made.
It takes about two tonnes of alumina to make one tonne of aluminium. In 1996 Bratsk produced 783,000 tonnes of refined aluminium and Krasnoyarsk 777,000 tonnes.
"We still have some shortfalls. Out of 1.5 million tonnes of alumina (for 1997), we still need 30,000 to 40,000 tonnes," Krasnoyarsk's Druzhinin said.
"We have basically covered our needs (for 1997)," Bratsk's Shlaifshtein added.
